e-7400.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14077889/assets/e5647c0f19727d1e626e637464cc57444e0bc0f2f8e99a4afd15d3c3631dc3f0.png)

Find an integral expression for the arc length of the polar curve $r=3-\sin(7\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi,$ shown in blue in the diagram above.
e-7400.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=3-\sin(7\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} =-7\cos(7\theta)
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(3-\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}+(-7\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+49{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{9-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+1+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{10-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\theta )+48{cos}^{2}⁡(7\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14077889/assets/0bb9e5e7315d4bcd5fc21700fdd2597f6d9b585a109145de53c6f94e9530eabf.png)

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2(1-\cos\theta)$ for $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ (shown in blue in the picture above).
e-641.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ is given by

$$
L =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1-\cos\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\sin\theta.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8-8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

We now use the half-angle formula $1-\cos\theta =2\sin^2\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)$ to give

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={-4\cdot 2(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡0) \\  & =-8(0-1) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

a

b

decision.explanation: Polar arc length is L=∫√(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ. Since r=cos(6θ), dr/dθ=−6sin(6θ), so the integrand is √(cos²(6θ)+36sin²(6θ)). Thus option b is correct.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{12}?$
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))^{2}+(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(6\theta )+36{sin}^{2}⁡(6\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=cos⁡(6θ) for 0≤θ≤π12?

a
6∫0π/12cos2⁡(6θ)+sin2⁡(6θ)dθ
b
∫0π/12cos2⁡(6θ)+36sin2⁡(6θ)dθ
c
∫0π/12sin2⁡(6θ)+6cos2⁡(6θ)dθ
d
6∫0π/12sin2⁡(6θ)−cos2⁡(6θ)dθ
e
∫0π/12cos2⁡(6θ)−6sin2⁡(6θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=cos⁡(6θ), we have drdθ=−6sin⁡(6θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/12(cos⁡(6θ))2+(−6sin⁡(6θ))2dθ=∫0π/12cos2⁡(6θ)+36sin2⁡(6θ)dθ.

content.knowledge_point: Creating an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Polar Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{12}?$
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))^{2}+(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /12}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(6\theta )+36{sin}^{2}⁡(6\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=θeθ for 0≤θ≤π2 (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
∫0π/2eθ2θ2+2θ+2dθ
b
∫0π/2eθ4θ2+2θ+1dθ
c

d
∫0π/2eθθ2+θ+1dθ
e
∫0π/2eθ2θ2+4θ+1dθ

decision.explanation: The polar arc length is ∫√(r²+(dr/dθ)²) dθ. For r=θe^θ, the product rule gives dr/dθ=e^θ(θ+1). Thus √(r²+(dr/dθ)²)=e^θ√(θ²+(θ+1)²)=e^θ√(2θ²+2θ+1), which matches option c.

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\theta {e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta {e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={e}^{\theta }+\theta {e}^{\theta }=(1+\theta ){e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\theta {e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{((1+\theta ){e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}{e}^{2\theta }+(1+2\theta +{\theta }^{2}){e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1){e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\theta }\sqrt{2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\theta {e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta {e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={e}^{\theta }+\theta {e}^{\theta }=(1+\theta ){e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(\theta {e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{((1+\theta ){e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}{e}^{2\theta }+(1+2\theta +{\theta }^{2}){e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{(2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1){e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{\theta }\sqrt{2{\theta }^{2}+2\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=1+2sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
∫0π5+4cos⁡θdθ
b
2∫0π1+sin⁡θdθ
c
2∫0π5+cos⁡θdθ
d
∫0π1+4sin⁡θdθ
e
∫0π5+4sin⁡θdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Polar arc length is ∫√(r²+(r′)²) dθ. Here r′=2cos(θ), so r²+(r′)²=(1+2sin(θ))²+4cos²(θ)=5+4sin(θ). Integrating from 0 to π gives option e.

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi $ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{5+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=1+2sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π (shown in blue in the diagram above)?

a
∫0π5+4cos⁡θdθ
b
2∫0π1+sin⁡θdθ
c

d
∫0π1+4sin⁡θdθ
e
∫0π5+4sin⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1+2sin⁡θ, we have drdθ=2cos⁡θ.

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π(1+2sin⁡θ)2+(2cos⁡θ)2dθ=∫0π1+4sin⁡θ+4sin2⁡θ+4cos2⁡θdθ=∫0π1+4sin⁡θ+4dθ=∫0π5+4sin⁡θdθ.

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi $ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{5+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=1+eθ for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
∫0π/2eθ+2e2θdθ
b
∫0π/22eθ+e2θdθ
c
∫0π/21+eθ+e2θdθ
d
∫0π/21+2e2θdθ
e
∫0π/21+2eθ+2e2θdθ
Submit

decision.explanation: Polar arc length is ∫√(r²+(r′)²) dθ. Since r=1+e^θ and r′=e^θ, r²+(r′)²=(1+e^θ)²+e^(2θ)=1+2e^θ+2e^(2θ). With bounds 0 to π/2, this matches option e.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+{e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(1+{e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{({e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+2{e}^{\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+2{e}^{\theta }+2{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

a

b

EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=1+eθ, we have drdθ=eθ.

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/2(1+eθ)2+(eθ)2dθ=∫0π/21+2eθ+e2θ+e2θdθ=∫0π/21+2eθ+2e2θdθ.

content.knowledge_point: Creating an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Polar Curve
content.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=1+{e}^{\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=1+{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }={e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{(1+{e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{({e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+2{e}^{\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{1+2{e}^{\theta }+2{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Polar arc length is ∫√(r²+(r′)²) dθ. For r=cos(2θ), r′=−2sin(2θ), giving √(cos²(2θ)+4sin²(2θ)). With bounds 0 to π/3, this is option b.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}?$
after.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve r=cos⁡(2θ) for 0≤θ≤π3?

a
∫0π/3sin2⁡(2θ)+4cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
∫0π/3cos2⁡(2θ)+4sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
c

e
∫0π/3sin2⁡(2θ)+2cos2⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The arc length L of a polar curve r=r(θ) is given by

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=cos⁡(2θ), we have

drdθ=−2sin⁡(2θ).

Therefore, the arc length is

L=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/3(cos⁡(2θ))2+(−2sin⁡(2θ))2dθ=∫0π/3cos2⁡(2θ)+4sin2⁡(2θ)dθ.

content.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}?$
content.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(2\theta )+4{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=3{e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{(3{e}^{\theta })}^{2}+{(3{e}^{\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{e}^{2\theta }+9{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{18{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{e}^{\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /4}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =3\sqrt{2}({e}^{\pi /4}-1).\end{aligned}
$$
